blocks.text: A chilled-water pump in a hospital plant runs at 1450 rpm at full duty. When the building load falls, the variable-speed drive slows the motor to 80 per cent of full speed. The pump does not simply do 80 per cent of the work: the flow falls to 80 per cent, but the electrical power it draws falls to about 51 per cent. Understanding why is the heart of pump performance and similarity.

blocks.markdown: A rotodynamic pump adds energy to a liquid by turning the impeller. Three quantities describe what it does: the **volume flow rate** $Q$ (m$^3$/s), the **head** $H$ (m of liquid column, the energy added per unit weight) and the **shaft power** $P$ (W) taken from the driver. Measured at several flow rates, they give the performance curves of the pump at one speed. The question for a designer is what happens to those curves when the speed $N$ changes, or when a different size of pump is considered.

blocks.title: Affinity laws
blocks.text: For one pump (fixed impeller diameter $D$) running at different speeds, with dynamically similar operating points and unchanged efficiency: flow is proportional to speed, head to speed squared and power to speed cubed. They follow from dimensional analysis: with $\rho$ the liquid density, the flow coefficient $Q/(ND^3)$, head coefficient $gH/(N^2D^2)$ and power coefficient $P/(\rho N^3 D^5)$ are held constant.

blocks.caption: Affinity laws for a change of speed at constant impeller diameter

blocks.title: Slowing a pump with the affinity laws
blocks.prompt: A pump at 1450 rpm delivers 0.05 m$^3$/s at a head of 32 m and absorbs 20.5 kW of shaft power. Predict the corresponding duty at 1160 rpm, assuming the efficiency is unchanged.

steps.text: Flow scales with the speed ratio.
Head scales with the square of the speed ratio.
Power scales with the cube of the speed ratio.

blocks.markdown: **Efficiency.** The useful power given to the liquid is the **hydraulic (water) power** $P_h=\rho g Q H$. The pump efficiency is the ratio of hydraulic power to the shaft power supplied: $\eta=P_h/P$. Because the affinity laws scale $Q H$ with $N^3$ and $P$ with $N^3$, efficiency is predicted to stay the same at corresponding points; in practice it falls a little at large speed changes because viscous effects do not scale perfectly. **Specific speed** combines $Q$, $H$ and $N$ into one dimensionless number that is independent of size, so it describes the *shape* of the impeller.

blocks.caption: Pump efficiency and dimensionless specific speed (omega in rad/s, evaluated at best efficiency point)

blocks.title: Efficiency and specific speed
blocks.prompt: A pump runs at 1450 rpm and delivers 0.04 m$^3$/s of water ($\rho=998$ kg/m$^3$) at a head of 25 m. The shaft power is 12.8 kW. Find the efficiency and the dimensionless specific speed.

steps.text: Efficiency is hydraulic over shaft power.

blocks.answer: $\eta\approx0.765$ (about 76.5%) and $\omega_s\approx0.49$, which is in the radial-flow (centrifugal) range.

blocks.caption: Typical ranges, shown for orientation only; boundaries vary between sources

items: Pick the best-efficiency duty of the machine; evaluate $\omega_s$ there with $\omega$ in rad/s and $H$ in metres.
Low $\omega_s$ means a narrow, large-diameter impeller delivering high head at low flow.
High $\omega_s$ means a wide, small-diameter impeller delivering low head at high flow.
Quote the same unit system when comparing: dimensional forms using rpm, m$^3$/s and m give different numbers.

blocks.title: Limits of the affinity laws
blocks.text: They hold only between dynamically similar points on one pump curve and for the same liquid. A pump working against a system with static head does not move along the system curve in proportion to speed, so matching the new duty to a given system needs the system curve (a later unit). The laws do not apply across large changes in Reynolds number.

points: At constant diameter and dynamic similarity, $Q\propto N$, $H\propto N^2$ and $P\propto N^3$.
Pump efficiency is hydraulic power $\rho g Q H$ divided by shaft power.
Dimensionless specific speed $\omega_s=\omega\sqrt Q/(gH)^{3/4}$ indicates impeller type: low for radial, high for axial machines.

questions.stem: A circulating pump has its impeller speed increased by 20% (same impeller, same liquid, similar operating point). By what factor does the shaft power change?

options.text: It increases by a factor of about 1.73
It increases by a factor of 1.20
It increases by a factor of 1.44
It increases by a factor of 2.07

questions.correctOptionText: It increases by a factor of about 1.73

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it cubes the speed ratio, and 1.2 cubed is about 1.73.
distractorRationale.b: Treats power as proportional to speed, which is the flow-rate law.
distractorRationale.c: Squares the speed ratio, which is the head law, not the power law.
distractorRationale.d: Over-applies the law with a fourth-power relation, which does not exist here.

questions.explanation: Power scales with the cube of speed, so the factor is $1.2^3=1.73$. Squaring would give the head ratio and the first power would give the flow ratio.

questions.stem: A pump produces 45 m of head at 2900 rpm. At a similar operating point at 2320 rpm with the same impeller, the head is closest to:

distractorRationale.a: Scales head linearly with speed, which is the flow law.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: it applies the square of the speed ratio 0.8.
distractorRationale.c: Uses the cube, which is the power law.
distractorRationale.d: Inverts the speed ratio, so it raises the head when speed is reduced.

questions.explanation: Head scales with the square of speed: $H_2=45\times(2320/2900)^2=28.8$ m. The other values come from using the wrong exponent or inverting the ratio, and a speed reduction must reduce head.

questions.stem: A dosing pump delivers liquid at a hydraulic power of 6.4 kW while the motor shaft supplies 8.0 kW. Its efficiency is:

distractorRationale.a: Inverts the ratio (shaft over hydraulic power), giving an impossible efficiency above 1.
distractorRationale.b: Has no basis in the data; it is not the ratio of the two powers.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: hydraulic power divided by shaft power.
distractorRationale.d: Takes the loss fraction (1.6 kW of 8.0 kW), not the efficiency.

questions.explanation: Efficiency is useful hydraulic power over shaft power: $6.4/8.0=0.80$. The 1.6 kW difference is the loss inside the pump, which is the 0.20 fraction.

questions.stem: A circulating pump runs at 1480 rpm and at its best efficiency point passes 0.30 m$^3$/s against a head of 20.0 m. Using the typical ranges given in the lesson, the dimensionless specific speed is about 1.62 and the suitable impeller type is:

distractorRationale.a: This type suits specific speeds below about 1.0, which would need a higher head per unit flow.
distractorRationale.b: Axial pumps suit specific speeds above about 2.5, so this duty is too high in head for one.
distractorRationale.c: Not a rotodynamic type, and specific speed is not used to select it.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: the specific speed of about 1.62 lies in the mixed-flow range.

questions.explanation: With $\omega=155$ rad/s, $\omega_s=\omega\sqrt Q/(gH)^{3/4}=1.62$. That falls between the radial and axial ranges, so a mixed-flow impeller is appropriate.

questions.stem: A student predicts the effect of slowing a pump using the affinity laws. Which statement is consistent with them (same pump, same liquid, similar operating points)?

options.text: Halving the speed cuts the head to a quarter and the shaft power to an eighth, while the efficiency is predicted to be unchanged
Halving the speed halves the head and quarters the shaft power
Halving the speed halves the head, the flow and the power
Halving the speed cuts the flow to a quarter and the efficiency to half

questions.correctOptionText: Halving the speed cuts the head to a quarter and the shaft power to an eighth, while the efficiency is predicted to be unchanged

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it uses the squared and cubed speed ratios and unchanged efficiency.
distractorRationale.b: Mixes up the exponents: head follows the square and power the cube of speed.
distractorRationale.c: Treats every quantity as linear in speed, which only holds for flow.
distractorRationale.d: Flow is linear in speed, and the laws predict unchanged efficiency.

questions.explanation: With $N_2/N_1=0.5$: $H_2/H_1=0.25$, $P_2/P_1=0.125$ and $Q_2/Q_1=0.5$. Since hydraulic power and shaft power both scale with $N^3$, the efficiency ratio is predicted to be 1.

questions.stem: Water ($\rho=998$ kg/m$^3$, $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$) is pumped at 0.030 m$^3$/s against a total head of 18.0 m by a pump of efficiency 0.72. Find the shaft power in kW.
questions.explanation: Hydraulic power is $\rho g Q H=998\times9.81\times0.030\times18.0=5286.8$ W. Dividing by the efficiency 0.72 gives the shaft power of 7.343 kW.

questions.stem: A pump absorbs 15.0 kW at 1750 rpm. Using the affinity laws, find the shaft power in kW when the speed is reduced to 1400 rpm, assuming similar operating points.
questions.explanation: Power scales with the cube of speed: $15.0\times(1400/1750)^3=15.0\times0.8^3=7.68$ kW. The reduction is far larger than the 20% speed change, which is why variable-speed drives save so much energy.

questions.stem: A boiler-feed pump runs at 2950 rpm and at best efficiency passes 0.012 m$^3$/s at a head of 60.0 m. Calculate the dimensionless specific speed $\omega_s=\omega\sqrt Q/(gH)^{3/4}$ (with $\omega$ in rad/s, $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$).
questions.explanation: Convert the speed: $\omega=2\pi\times2950/60=308.9$ rad/s. Then $\omega_s=308.9\times\sqrt{0.012}/(9.81\times60)^{0.75}=0.283$, which is in the radial range, so a centrifugal impeller is appropriate.

questions.stem: A pump delivers a variable flow in a closed pipework loop with no static head. Compare throttling a valve with reducing the pump speed to cut the delivered flow to 70% of the design value. Use the affinity laws to estimate the shaft power in the speed-control case and explain why it saves energy.
markingGuide: States Q proportional to N, so speed ratio 0.7
Power proportional to N cubed gives 0.7^3 = 0.343, about 34% of design power (assuming unchanged efficiency)
Identifies that a throttle keeps speed and head capability high and dissipates the surplus head as loss in the valve
Notes that hydraulic power needed is rho g Q H with a lower H at lower speed, so speed control delivers less head
Mentions the caveat that efficiency and similarity hold approximately and drive/motor losses also matter
questions.explanation: In a friction-dominated loop the system head falls with flow squared, which is exactly how head scales with speed, so the pump stays near its best efficiency as it slows: power falls to $0.7^3\approx0.34$ of design. A throttle leaves the pump at full speed and burns the excess head across the valve, so power falls much less.

questions.stem: Explain, in terms of impeller shape and the direction of the flow through it, why a low-specific-speed pump is a radial centrifugal machine while a high-specific-speed pump is axial. State which of head and flow each type is best suited to.
markingGuide: Defines specific speed as dimensionless combination of speed, flow and head, independent of size, describing impeller shape
Low specific speed: high head and low flow, narrow impeller of large diameter with flow leaving radially, head generated mainly by centrifugal action
High specific speed: low head and high flow, wide impeller of small diameter relative to flow area, flow stays axial
Notes that choice is by specific speed at the best efficiency point to maximise efficiency
questions.explanation: Because $\omega_s\propto\sqrt Q/H^{3/4}$, a high head per unit flow gives a low value and requires the large radius change of a centrifugal impeller, while a large flow at small head gives a high value and is passed with little radius change by an axial impeller.
